docs.title: Controls Crash Course
docs.text: A course on control theory and robot control, from a mass-spring-damper to a walking humanoid.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This is a crash course. Each chapter covers the minimum needed to understand its topic and leaves out detail you'd need to master it. Every chapter has whole textbooks behind it; we skip most of that material to keep the course manageable.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: The course is written for computer science students and graduates, but anyone can use it. It assumes algebra and trigonometry. Calculus helps, and Chapter 0 covers the math the course uses. The labs assume some familiarity with programming, but feel free to ask your favorite LLM to assist you with the examples.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The course ends with whole-body control of a walking humanoid. Before that, Chapter 7 builds the control loop for a simulated 7-DOF arm, using MuJoCo for physics, Pinocchio for the robot model, and TSID for torques.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
• Read the chapters in order.
  • Chapter 0 is optional. If it's too much, skip it; later chapters link back to the parts they use.
  • Use the widgets to try out the ideas in each chapter.
  • Labs will be added once the lab environment is ready.

Chapters 2–8 are in progress.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
• 0. Math Toolkit: complex numbers, linear algebra, and differential equations, kept to what the course uses. Later chapters link back here with short refreshers.
  • 1. Time Domain: dynamic systems and state space, stability, and linearization.
  • 2. Frequency Domain (coming soon): the Laplace transform, transfer functions, poles and zeros, and Bode plots.
  • 3. Feedback and Joint Control (coming soon): PID control, root locus, and stability margins.
  • 4. Kinematics (coming soon): rotations and transforms, forward kinematics, the Jacobian, singularities, inverse kinematics, and redundancy.
  • 5. Rigid-Body Dynamics (coming soon): the manipulator equations, Pinocchio's algorithms, and computed-torque control.
  • 6. Task-Space Control (coming soon): operational-space control, null-space projection, and impedance control.
  • 7. Task-Space Inverse Dynamics (coming soon): multiple tasks and hard limits as a quadratic program, on a 7-DOF arm.
  • 8. Whole-Body Control (coming soon): floating bases, contacts, and balance, on a walking humanoid.

docs.title: State Space, Stability, and Linearization
docs.text: A robot arm has dozens of coupled equations of motion, so we need one uniform form that software can handle. That form is state space.

docs.title: From one equation to many
docs.text:
Give every derivative except the highest its own name. For the mass-spring-damper, let \(x_1 = x\) (position) and \(x_2 = \dot{x}\) (velocity):

\[ \dot{x}_1 = x_2, \qquad \dot{x}_2 = -\frac{k}{m}x_1 - \frac{b}{m}x_2 + \frac{1}{m}u \]

An \(N\)th-order equation always becomes \(N\) first-order equations this way.

docs.title: The matrix form
docs.text:
Refresher

A matrix times a vector takes the dot product of each row with the vector. See Vectors and Matrices.

Stack the states into a vector \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1,\ x_2]^T\) (bold, to tell it apart from the displacement \(x\)):

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} + Bu, \qquad y = C\mathbf{x} + Du \] \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -k/m & -b/m \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1/m \end{bmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = 0 \]
  • \(A\) holds the system's own dynamics.
  • \(B\) says how the input pushes the state.
  • \(C\) picks out the measured output, here the position. \(D\) is a direct path from input to output, usually zero.

A 7-joint arm needs bigger matrices, but the equation keeps the same shape.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text:
Refresher

The solution of \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}\) is a sum of modes \(e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}\), one per eigenvalue of \(A\). See Differential Equations.

The eigenvalues of the mass-spring-damper's \(A\) are the roots of

\[ \det(sI - A) = s^2 + \frac{b}{m}s + \frac{k}{m} = 0 \]

which is the characteristic equation from the previous page, divided by \(m\). So the eigenvalues of \(A\) are the characteristic roots, and they decide how the system behaves:

  • Every eigenvalue has a negative real part: the system returns to rest. It's stable.
  • Any eigenvalue has a positive real part: some motion grows without bound. It's unstable.
  • Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis, with none to the right: it oscillates forever without growing or decaying, like the undamped spring.

In the complex plane, stable means every eigenvalue sits in the left half. This figure from Complex Numbers shows the motion each location produces, and that eigenvalues farther left decay faster:

In code, that's one call:

#include <Eigen/Dense>

const double m = 1.0, b = 1.0, k = 10.0;
Eigen::Matrix2d A;
A << 0.0,    1.0,
     -k / m, -b / m;
Eigen::EigenSolver<Eigen::Matrix2d> solver(A);
// solver.eigenvalues() = -0.5 ± 3.12j: negative real parts, so stable

docs.title: Linearization
docs.text:
Refresher

Near a point, \(\mathbf{f}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \delta\mathbf{x}) \approx \mathbf{f}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) + J\,\delta\mathbf{x}\), where \(J\) is the Jacobian. See Partial Derivatives and Jacobians.

Real systems are nonlinear: \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, u)\). Near an equilibrium, a state where \(\mathbf{f} = 0\) and nothing changes, they behave almost linearly, with \(A\) equal to the Jacobian \(\partial\mathbf{f}/\partial\mathbf{x}\) there.

A pendulum of length \(l\) with mass \(m\) at its tip, pivot friction \(b\), and motor torque \(\tau\) follows

\[ ml^2\ddot{\theta} + b\dot{\theta} + mgl\sin\theta = \tau \]

The figure shows both equilibria: hanging down, where gravity pulls it back, and balanced upright, where gravity pulls it away.

Linearizing around an angle \(\bar{\theta}\) gives

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\dfrac{g}{l}\cos\bar{\theta} & -\dfrac{b}{ml^2} \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Hanging down (\(\bar{\theta} = 0\)): the bottom-left entry is \(-g/l\), just like the spring's \(-k/m\). Gravity acts as a spring, the eigenvalues have negative real parts, and the pendulum is stable.
  • Balanced upright (\(\bar{\theta} = \pi\)): the entry flips to \(+g/l\). The characteristic equation becomes \(s^2 + \frac{b}{ml^2}s - \frac{g}{l} = 0\), which always has one positive real root. The pendulum is unstable: it falls.

The approximation only holds near the equilibrium, which is why controllers built on it work best when they keep the system close to its operating point.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Franklin, Powell, and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems. It writes state space as \(F, G, H, J\) where we use \(A, B, C, D\).
  • Spong, Hutchinson, and Vidyasagar, Robot Modeling and Control, whose notation this course follows.

Lab: time_domain (coming soon)

The C++ lab simulates the mass-spring-damper open loop and logs its step and impulse responses to Rerun.

docs.title: Dynamic Systems
docs.text: A dynamic system is one whose output depends on its history, not just its current input. Push a cart and let go: it keeps rolling. We describe such systems with differential equations, in terms of an input \(u\) we act on (a force, a torque), an output \(y\) we measure, and a state: the smallest set of variables that, together with future inputs, determines the future.

docs.title: First-order systems
docs.text:
A cart of mass \(m\) is pushed with force \(u\) against viscous drag \(-bv\):

\[ m\dot{v} + bv = u \]

Refresher

\(\dot{x} = ax\) has the solution \(x(0)e^{at}\), which decays when \(a < 0\). See Differential Equations.

With no push, the speed decays as \(e^{-t/\tau}\), where \(\tau = m/b\) is the time constant. With a constant push, the speed rises toward \(u/b\) along the curve in the figure. It covers 63% of the way after one time constant and is essentially done after four.

docs.title: Second-order systems
docs.text:
Add a spring and the system can store energy in two places, as motion and as spring stretch, and trade it back and forth. That's what makes oscillation possible.

In the figure, a block of mass \(m\) is connected to a wall by a spring of stiffness \(k\) and a damper with coefficient \(b\). The spring pulls back with force \(-kx\), the damper resists motion with \(-b\dot{x}\), and we push with \(u\). Newton's second law gives

\[ m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = u \]

You solved this equation in Differential Equations. Its characteristic roots are clearest when written with two new quantities:

\[ s = -\zeta\omega_n \pm \omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1}, \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{km}} \]

The natural frequency \(\omega_n\) (rad/s) sets how fast the system moves. The damping ratio \(\zeta\) decides what kind of roots it has, and so how the motion dies out:

Damping ratio Roots Behavior \(\zeta = 0\) \(\pm j\omega_n\) Undamped: oscillates forever. \(0 < \zeta < 1\) complex pair, \(-\zeta\omega_n \pm j\omega_d\) Underdamped: oscillates with a decaying envelope. \(\zeta = 1\) one repeated real root Critically damped: fastest return to rest without overshooting. \(\zeta > 1\) two negative real roots Overdamped: creeps back to rest without oscillating.

Here \(\omega_d = \omega_n\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}\) is the frequency it actually oscillates at. The figure shows the roots moving as \(\zeta\) increases, with \(\omega_n\) fixed:

Refresher

A complex pair \(\sigma \pm j\omega\) gives a solution \(e^{\sigma t}\cos\omega t\): an oscillation at \(\omega\) inside an envelope that decays when \(\sigma < 0\). See Complex Numbers.

A robot joint under feedback control behaves much like this system, so it's worth building a feel for it.

docs.title: Impulse response
docs.text:
An impulse is a sharp strike, like a hammer tap. Its size \(J\) is the force integrated over the strike, and it changes the block's velocity instantly by \(\Delta v = J/m\). The block then rings at \(\omega_d\) inside an envelope that decays at rate \(\zeta\omega_n\).

The impulse response formula

Starting from rest, an underdamped block struck with impulse \(J\) moves as

\[ x(t) = \frac{J}{m\,\omega_d}\, e^{-\zeta\omega_n t} \sin(\omega_d t) \]

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
The block has mass \(m = 1\text{ kg}\), and each press of Impulse adds \(1.5\) m/s to its velocity. Change \(k\) and \(b\) at any time, even mid-swing. (The widget solves the equation numerically; Chapter 5 explains how simulators do this.)

  • Set \(b = 0\). It oscillates forever.
  • For \(k = 10\) N/m, find the \(b\) that gives critical damping.
  • With \(b = 0\), press Impulse in time with the swing. That's resonance.
Spring constant k = N/m Damping coefficient b = N·s/m Impulse

docs.title: Complex Numbers
docs.text: Control theory describes oscillation with complex numbers. You need four facts.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
Engineers write \(j = \sqrt{-1}\) (reserving \(i\) for electric current). A complex number \(z = a + jb\) has a real part \(a\) and an imaginary part \(b\), and you can picture it as the point \((a, b)\) on the complex plane.

Arithmetic works as usual, with \(j^2 = -1\):

\[ (1 + 2j)(3 - j) = 3 - j + 6j - 2j^2 = 5 + 5j \]

The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part: \(\bar{z} = a - jb\).

docs.title: Polar form
docs.text:
The same point can be described by its distance from the origin and its angle:

\[ |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \angle z = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a) \]

In the figure, \(a\) and \(b\) are the point's coordinates, \(|z|\) is its distance from the origin, and the angle is measured from the real axis. The conjugate is the mirror image across the real axis.

docs.title: Euler's formula
docs.text:
\[ e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta \]

So any complex number can be written \(z = |z|\,e^{j\angle z}\). Multiplying two complex numbers then multiplies their magnitudes and adds their angles.

docs.title: Complex exponentials in time
docs.text:
Let \(s = \sigma + j\omega\). Then

\[ e^{st} = e^{\sigma t}\, e^{j\omega t} \]

is a point rotating around the origin at \(\omega\) rad/s, with a radius \(e^{\sigma t}\) that shrinks or grows. Adding a conjugate pair cancels the imaginary parts and leaves a real signal:

\[ e^{st} + e^{\bar{s}t} = 2e^{\sigma t}\cos\omega t \]

That's a cosine whose amplitude follows \(e^{\sigma t}\). The dotted envelope is a plain first-order exponential decay, and the oscillation stays inside it:

The figure below shows the signal produced by an \(s\) in each part of the plane. The faint dots below the axis are the conjugate partners of the ones above.

The real part of \(s\) decides decay or growth, and the imaginary part decides oscillation. This picture comes back throughout the course.

In C++, std::complex<double> provides all of this, including std::abs, std::arg, and std::exp.

docs.title: Derivatives
docs.text:
The derivative of \(x(t)\) is its instantaneous rate of change, the slope of its graph: \(dx/dt\). Time derivatives are written with dots: \(\dot{x}\) for the first derivative, \(\ddot{x}\) for the second. If \(x\) is position, \(\dot{x}\) is velocity and \(\ddot{x}\) is acceleration.

The rules you'll need:

Function Derivative \(t^n\) \(n t^{n-1}\) \(e^{at}\) \(a e^{at}\) \(\sin \omega t\) \(\omega \cos \omega t\) \(\cos \omega t\) \(-\omega \sin \omega t\) \(f(t)\,g(t)\) (product rule) \(\dot{f} g + f \dot{g}\) \(f(g(t))\) (chain rule) \(f'(g(t))\,\dot{g}(t)\)

Derivatives are also linear: the derivative of \(a f + b g\) is \(a\dot{f} + b\dot{g}\).

docs.title: Integrals
docs.text:
The integral accumulates a quantity over time, the area under its graph. It undoes the derivative:

\[ \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \dot{x}\, dt = x(t_1) - x(t_0) \]

Integrate velocity and you get the change in position. Integrate force over a short strike and you get the impulse, the change in momentum.

docs.title: The software view
docs.text:
On a computer, both become simple loops over small time steps \(\Delta t\):

\[ \dot{x}(t_k) \approx \frac{x_{k+1} - x_k}{\Delta t}, \qquad \int f\, dt \approx \sum_k f(t_k)\, \Delta t \]

docs.title: Differential Equations
docs.text: A differential equation relates a function to its own derivatives. Its solution is a whole function, not a number, and pinning down a single solution takes one initial condition per order: a starting value for \(x\), plus one for \(\dot{x}\) if the equation involves \(\ddot{x}\), and so on.

docs.title: First order
docs.text:
\[ \dot{x} = ax \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x(t) = x(0)\, e^{at} \]

Check it: the derivative of \(x(0)e^{at}\) is \(a\,x(0)e^{at} = ax\). The solution decays to zero if \(a < 0\) and grows if \(a > 0\).

docs.title: Second order
docs.text:
Here's the equation of a mass-spring-damper; Chapter 1 explains the physics. For now, just solve it:

\[ m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = 0 \]

Guess \(x = e^{st}\). Substituting gives \((ms^2 + bs + k)\,e^{st} = 0\), which holds when

\[ ms^2 + bs + k = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad s = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4mk}}{2m} \]

This is the characteristic equation, and its two roots decide the solution:

Roots Solution Two different real roots \(s_1, s_2\) \(x = c_1 e^{s_1 t} + c_2 e^{s_2 t}\) One repeated real root \(s\) \(x = (c_1 + c_2 t)\, e^{st}\) Complex pair \(\sigma \pm j\omega\) \(x = e^{\sigma t}(c_1 \cos\omega t + c_2 \sin\omega t)\)

The constants \(c_1, c_2\) come from the initial conditions. As in Complex Numbers, the real part of each root decides decay or growth, and an imaginary part means oscillation. If every root has a negative real part, the solution decays to zero.

docs.title: Systems of equations
docs.text:
Several first-order equations together form a vector equation:

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} \]

If \(A\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) with eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_i\), the solution is

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots \]

Each eigenvector is a mode that evolves on its own, at a rate set by its eigenvalue. For the matrix in the eigenvalue example, the modes are \(e^{-t}\) and \(e^{-2t}\): both decay. Same rule as before: if every eigenvalue has a negative real part, the solution decays to zero.

Equations with an input, such as \(m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = u(t)\), are handled in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
docs.text:
Multiplying a vector by a matrix usually changes its direction. An eigenvector of \(A\) is a special vector whose direction doesn't change; it only gets scaled:

\[ A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} \]

The scale factor \(\lambda\) is the eigenvalue that goes with \(\mathbf{v}\).

docs.title: Finding them
docs.text:
Rearranging gives \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = 0\). A nonzero \(\mathbf{v}\) can only solve this if \(A - \lambda I\) is singular, so the eigenvalues are the roots of

\[ \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \]

This is a polynomial in \(\lambda\), the characteristic polynomial. An \(n \times n\) matrix has \(n\) eigenvalues (counting repeats). They can be complex; for a real matrix, complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. Each eigenvector lies in the null space of \(A - \lambda I\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = (\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 2) \]

So \(\lambda_1 = -1\) and \(\lambda_2 = -2\). Solving \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = 0\) for each gives

\[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

The figure shows \(A\) acting on both eigenvectors and on one other vector, \(\mathbf{w} = [1,\ 0]^T\). Each eigenvector stays on its own line; the eigenvalues here are negative, so both flip. \(\mathbf{w}\) lands on a different line.

docs.title: Why they matter
docs.text:
Along an eigenvector, a matrix acts like plain multiplication by a number. That makes eigenvalues the key to systems of differential equations: in Differential Equations, each eigenvalue becomes an exponential \(e^{\lambda t}\) in the solution.

In Eigen: Eigen::EigenSolver<Eigen::MatrixXd> solver(A); solver.eigenvalues();

docs.title: Partial derivatives
docs.text:
For a function of several variables, the partial derivative with respect to one of them is the rate of change when only that variable moves and the rest are held fixed:

\[ f(x, y) = x^2 y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x^2 \]

docs.title: Linear approximation
docs.text:
Near a point, a smooth function looks like a straight line (or a flat plane). For one variable,

\[ f(\bar{x} + \delta x) \approx f(\bar{x}) + f'(\bar{x})\,\delta x \]

For example, \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) near \(\theta = 0\):

The dashed tangent line and the curve are almost identical inside the shaded band, and drift apart outside it. With several variables, each one contributes its own partial derivative times its own small change.

docs.title: The Jacobian
docs.text:
For a function that takes a vector in and gives a vector out, collect all the partial derivatives into a matrix, the Jacobian:

\[ J_{ij} = \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}, \qquad \mathbf{f}(\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \delta\mathbf{x}) \approx \mathbf{f}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) + J\,\delta\mathbf{x} \]

Each row is an output and each column is an input. The Jacobian answers: if I nudge the inputs a little, how do the outputs move?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Converting polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) to a position \((r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)\):

\[ J = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \det J = r \]

A small circle of input changes around a point maps to an ellipse of position changes. It's stretched by \(r\) in the \(\theta\) direction, because turning by \(\theta\) moves the point along an arc of radius \(r\):

At \(r = 0\) the determinant is zero, so \(J\) is singular: the ellipse collapses to a line, and changing \(\theta\) does nothing to the position. A robot arm's Jacobian works the same way, and Chapter 4 is about exactly these situations.

docs.title: Solving Linear Systems
docs.text:
Many problems in this course come down to: given a matrix \(A\) and a vector \(\mathbf{b}\), find \(\mathbf{x}\) such that

\[ A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \]

If \(A\) is \(m \times n\), it takes inputs \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(n\) entries and produces outputs with \(m\) entries. Whether this equation has a solution, and how many, depends on four sets of vectors that every matrix comes with.

docs.title: The four subspaces
docs.text:
On the output side:

  • The column space \(C(A)\), also called the range or image, is the set of all outputs \(A\mathbf{x}\) can produce. Its dimension is the rank \(r\) of \(A\).
  • The left null space \(N(A^T)\) holds the output directions \(A\) can never produce. Its dimension is \(m - r\).

On the input side:

  • The null space \(N(A)\), also called the kernel, is the set of inputs \(A\) maps to zero: all \(\mathbf{n}\) with \(A\mathbf{n} = 0\). Its dimension is \(n - r\).
  • The row space \(C(A^T)\) is every combination of the rows of \(A\). Its dimension is also \(r\).

Each shape in the figure above stands for a whole space of vectors through the origin: a line, a plane, or a higher-dimensional version. On each side the two spaces are at right angles: every vector in one is perpendicular to every vector in the other. On the input side, this follows from \(A\mathbf{n} = 0\), which says each row of \(A\) has a zero dot product with \(\mathbf{n}\). Their dimensions also add up to the full space, so every vector is a sum of one piece from each.

For example, \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) keeps the first two entries of \(\mathbf{x}\) and drops the third. Its row space is the \(xy\)-plane and its null space is the \(z\)-axis, as in the figure below:

The dashed lines split the input \(\mathbf{x}\) into its part in the plane, \(\mathbf{x}_r\) (blue), and its part along the line, \(\mathbf{x}_n\) (orange). \(A\) keeps \(\mathbf{x}_r\) and discards \(\mathbf{x}_n\), so \(A\mathbf{x} = A\mathbf{x}_r\).

A matrix is full rank when \(r\) is as large as its shape allows, the smaller of \(m\) and \(n\). The example above is full rank: its rank is 2, so it reaches every point in its 2D output space. Add a row of zeros, giving \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), and it does the same thing, but its outputs now live in 3D. It still only reaches the \(xy\)-plane, so its rank of 2 falls short of 3: it isn't full rank, and its left null space is the \(z\)-axis, the outputs it can never produce. A full-rank \(3 \times 3\) matrix, by contrast, reaches all of 3D space and discards nothing.

docs.title: What this means for solving
docs.text:
• A solution exists only if \(\mathbf{b}\) is in the column space.
  • If the null space contains anything besides zero, solutions aren't unique: if \(\mathbf{x}\) solves \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), so does \(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n}\) for any \(\mathbf{n}\) in the null space.

docs.title: Square matrices: the inverse and the determinant
docs.text:
A square matrix is invertible when its null space is just zero. Then there's a matrix \(A^{-1}\) with \(A^{-1}A = I\), and every \(\mathbf{b}\) has exactly one solution, \(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\).

In code

Don't form the inverse explicitly. Ask a solver instead, which is faster and more accurate: Eigen::VectorXd x = A.colPivHouseholderQr().solve(b);

The determinant tests this with a single number. For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix,

\[ \det \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc \]

Geometrically, it's how much \(A\) scales area (or volume). If \(\det A = 0\), the null space contains a nonzero vector, so different inputs produce the same output, the input can't be recovered, and \(A\) has no inverse. Such a matrix is singular.

For example, in \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) the second column is twice the first. Its determinant is \(1 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2 = 0\), its rank is 1, and \([2,\ -1]^T\) is in its null space. The figure shows the unit square mapped by an invertible matrix and by this singular one. The middle panel's matrix has determinant 2.5, so it scales the square's area by 2.5.

docs.title: The pseudo-inverse
docs.text:
When \(A\) isn't square, or is singular, the pseudo-inverse \(A^+\) still gives the best available answer, \(\mathbf{x} = A^+\mathbf{b}\). In terms of the four subspaces:

  • If \(\mathbf{b}\) isn't in the column space, there's no exact solution. \(A^+\) solves for the closest point in the column space, where the error to \(\mathbf{b}\) is perpendicular, as in the figure below. That makes \(|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}|\) as small as possible. This is the least-squares solution. For a tall, full-rank \(A\), \(A^+ = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T\).
  • If the null space isn't just zero, there are infinitely many solutions. \(A^+\) picks the one with no null-space part, which lies entirely in the row space and has the smallest \(|\mathbf{x}|\). For a wide, full-rank \(A\), \(A^+ = A^T(AA^T)^{-1}\).

The first case, least squares, looks like this:

In Eigen: A.completeOrthogonalDecomposition().pseudoInverse().

docs.title: Quadratic forms
docs.text:
For a symmetric matrix \(Q\), the expression \(\mathbf{x}^T Q \mathbf{x}\) is a single number, a quadratic form. It's the matrix version of \(qx^2\). Kinetic energy is one: for a single mass it's \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), and for a robot arm it's \(\tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T M \dot{\mathbf{q}}\).

\(Q\) is positive definite if \(\mathbf{x}^T Q \mathbf{x} > 0\) for every nonzero \(\mathbf{x}\). Equivalently, all its eigenvalues are positive. Its graph is a bowl with a single lowest point. A matrix with eigenvalues of both signs gives a saddle instead. Along some directions a saddle curves up, along others down, so it has no minimum:

docs.title: Minimizing a quadratic
docs.text:
To minimize

\[ f(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^T Q \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x} \]

with \(Q\) positive definite, set every partial derivative to zero. That gives a linear system, \(Q\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}\), with one solution: the bottom of the bowl in the figure.

docs.title: Least squares
docs.text:
When \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) has no exact solution, minimize the error \(|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}|^2\) instead. This is a quadratic, and setting its derivatives to zero gives

\[ A^TA\,\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

whose solution is the pseudo-inverse answer from Solving Linear Systems. Adding a penalty \(\lambda^2|\mathbf{x}|^2\) that keeps \(\mathbf{x}\) small gives

\[ (A^TA + \lambda^2 I)\,\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

which always has a solution, even when \(A\) is singular. This damped least squares returns in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Quadratic programs
docs.text: A quadratic program (QP) minimizes a quadratic subject to linear constraints: equalities \(E\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d}\) and inequalities \(G\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{h}\). With inequalities there's no formula; solvers search for the answer iteratively. Chapter 7's whole-body controller solves a QP every control cycle.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
A vector is an ordered list of numbers, written as a column and in bold: \(\mathbf{a} = [a_1,\ a_2,\ a_3]^T\).

The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up:

\[ \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3 = |\mathbf{a}|\,|\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between them. A dot product of zero means the vectors are perpendicular.

The cross product exists only in 3D. It gives a vector perpendicular to both inputs, with length \(|\mathbf{a}|\,|\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\) and direction given by the right-hand rule:

\[ \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2 \\ a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3 \\ a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 \end{bmatrix} \]

On the left, the dot product measures how much of \(\mathbf{b}\) lies along \(\mathbf{a}\). On the right, the cross product points straight out of the plane of \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), and its length is the shaded area.

docs.title: Matrices
docs.text:
A matrix is a grid of numbers. An \(m \times n\) matrix has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns.

Multiplying a matrix by a vector takes the dot product of each row with the vector:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 6 \\ 3 \cdot 5 + 4 \cdot 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 17 \\ 39 \end{bmatrix} \]

Shapes must line up: an \(m \times n\) matrix times an \(n\)-vector gives an \(m\)-vector.

The product \(AB\) means "apply \(B\), then \(A\)." Order matters: in general \(AB \neq BA\).

The transpose \(A^T\) swaps rows and columns. The identity \(I\) has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so \(I\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}\).

docs.title: In code
docs.text:
#include <Eigen/Dense>

Eigen::Vector3d a(1, 0, 0), b(0, 1, 0);
double d = a.dot(b);            // 0: perpendicular
Eigen::Vector3d c = a.cross(b); // (0, 0, 1)

Eigen::Matrix2d A;
A << 1, 2,
     3, 4;
Eigen::Vector2d y = A * Eigen::Vector2d(5, 6);  // (17, 39)
Eigen::Matrix2d At = A.transpose();
